note: Mock content for the prototype. The ship and its history are invented.

core.text: This is the Marigold's compass. It sat in a wooden stand in front of the ship's wheel, so the person steering could always see it.
The dial floats in a bowl of liquid, so it stays level and steady even when the ship rolls in heavy seas. The liquid was partly alcohol, so it would not freeze.
Out of sight of land, the compass, a clock and a few careful sums were all the crew had to know where they were.

open_question.text: How do you think they steered at night?

additions.text: Look at the dial: north is marked with a small decorated flower called a fleur-de-lis, a tradition that goes back hundreds of years.
To go a bit deeper: iron on the ship pulls the needle off true. The two iron balls on either side of the stand were moved until they cancelled that pull out.
At night a small oil lamp inside the stand lit the dial from below, so whoever was steering could read it without spoiling their night vision.
You can see where the compass stood on the model of the Marigold, just in front of the wheel at the back of the ship.

qa.text: It does. The needle still points north, more than 170 years later.
It's a mix of water and alcohol. The alcohol stops it freezing, and the liquid damps the swing of the dial.

qa_fallback.text: That's a good question, and I don't know the answer. What we do know is that this compass guided the Marigold for almost thirty years.
